chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from al-Barqi, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon them) who said:

I asked him about the person in Ihram who shades himself. He said: Is it due to an illness/cause? I said: The heat of the sun harms him while he is in Ihram. He said: It is a cause; he may shade himself and offer the ransom.

key_terms.عِلَّةٌ: A valid cause or excuse in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.مُحْرِمٌ: A person in the state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.وَيَفْدِي: And he offers the ransom (fidyah) for the exemption
key_terms.يُظَلِّلُ: To shade oneself (a prohibited act in Ihram unless excused)

ai.seo_question: Can a person in Ihram shade themselves from the sun if it causes harm, and what is the required compensation?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies that the heat of the sun constitutes a valid 'illah' (excuse) for a muhrim to shade their body, distinguishing it from mere preference. This ruling underscores the principle of *raf' al-haraj* (removal of hardship) in Islamic jurisprudence, where the necessity of relief from harm permits the temporary suspension of Ihram restrictions, provided the fidyah is paid. The dialogue highlights the practical application of legal reasoning in balancing ritual purity with physical comfort during pilgrimage.
